analysis.one_liner: Bars mortgage servicers from foreclosing while a homeowner's loan modification application is pending and penalizes servicers for slow or wrongful denials.
analysis.headline: The Mortgage Modification Reform Act of 2010 never received a vote: it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in March 2010, drew no cosponsors, and died there when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have protected homeowners applying for federal mortgage modifications. Servicers could not start or continue a foreclosure while a modification application was still pending, would have to decide applications within three months in the order received, and could not charge late fees while an application was pending. Servicers that wrongly denied or delayed applications would face Treasury penalties and smaller government incentive payments.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners struggling to keep their homes would gain. The bill would stop a servicer from starting or continuing a foreclosure while a loan modification application (for example, under the Home Affordable Modification Program) is still being evaluated, guarantee a decision within three months, require applications to be processed in order received, ban delinquency fees while an application is pending, and create a Treasury review process with penalties for wrongful denials of modifications [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Blocks servicers from initiating or continuing a foreclosure while a modification application filed before or within 30 days of the foreclosure notice is still under review.
Requires a servicer to decide each application within three months, in the order received, so homeowners get an answer instead of an open-ended wait.
Prohibits delinquency fees on homeowners while their modification application is pending, so the wait does not add to their debt.
Creates a Treasury process for homeowners to challenge wrongful denials of trial or permanent modifications, with mandatory penalties on servicers that deny applications improperly.

Cuts servicers' incentive payments 10% for each month past the three-month deadline, with 25% across-the-board cuts if fewer than 75% of applications are evaluated on time or fewer than 70% of trial modifications convert to permanent ones.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage servicers — many of them units of large banks — would pay. The bill requires them to evaluate modification applications within three months and in the order received, bars them from charging delinquency fees while an application is pending, blocks foreclosures while a modification is under review, and cuts their Treasury incentive payments 10% per month late, with a 25% cut if too few of their applications are processed on time [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Mortgage servicers and their bank owners

drawbacks.text: The bill relies entirely on Treasury's administrative machinery — it creates review processes and payment penalties but no private right of action, so a homeowner could not sue a servicer directly under it.
Barring foreclosure while any timely application is pending could extend the process for homeowners with no realistic prospect of qualifying, delaying resolution for investors and neighborhoods.
The bill offered no explanation or evidence for the 75% and 70% on-time benchmarks or the 25% penalty size, leaving significant discretion to the Treasury Secretary to define compliance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are concrete and targeted at a well-documented problem of the period — homeowners being foreclosed on while their modification applications sat unprocessed, and trial modifications never converting to permanent ones. The costs fall almost entirely on servicers through smaller federal incentive payments and penalties, not on taxpayers generally. The main weakness is design: the bill leans on Treasury enforcement rather than giving homeowners their own day in court, and its benchmarks were set without supporting analysis in the bill text. On balance, for the homeowners it covers, the benefits clearly outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Banking Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress expired, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 24, 2010, read twice, and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
It attracted no cosponsors in either chamber.
The committee took no further action, and no Senate vote ever occurred before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage servicers and the banks that own them are better off, because none of the timing rules, foreclosure stops, delinquency-fee bans, or payment cuts ever took effect. Homeowners navigating modification applications were left without the protections the bill would have provided.

for.name: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after its referral; no hearings, markup, or floor vote occurred before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no opposition is recorded; the bill died in committee with no cosponsors, so no party split is visible.

industries.note: Servicers running federal modification programs would face new duties and real money on the line: incentive payments cut 10% per month for slow evaluations, 25% cuts for missing processing benchmarks, and penalties for wrongful denials. During the foreclosure crisis, servicers were widely criticized for reviewing modifications and foreclosing at the same time, a practice the bill's foreclosure bar targets.

Bank-owned servicing arms would bear the same penalties and payment reductions, and banks holding the underlying mortgages would face more completed modifications and fewer foreclosures, which can reduce recoveries on delinquent loans.
The bill would build qualified housing counselors into the new review process for denied modification applications, giving them a formal reporting role.
